message.content: The pink monopoly is live and unbuilt; the last build failed only because the houses were not interleaved. Building the 3-2-2 spike now.
message.reasoning:
I need to make a legal Monopoly move. The previous action was rejected for building across the group without completing the set first.

I have the pink monopoly group: St. Charles Place, States Avenue, and Virginia Avenue. All are unmortgaged with zero houses. I also hold mortgaged properties including St. James Place, B&O Railroad, and Pennsylvania Avenue.

The previous build attempt failed because it tried to place three houses on Virginia Avenue, two on States Avenue, and two on St. Charles Place in a single operation without interleaving the purchases across the group.

The engine likely applies each house purchase in sequence. Building three houses on Virginia first would leave it far ahead of the other two properties, which would be illegal. I need to interleave purchases so no property leads by more than one house at any point.

I will interleave the purchases as one house on St. Charles, then States, then Virginia, repeating until Virginia reaches three houses. This satisfies the even-building rule. The plan costs $700 and leaves $26 cash. I am checking the rent values for each house level on the pink properties.

Virginia Avenue's rent is $500 with three houses, while St. Charles and States are only $150 each. Building seven houses would leave just $26 cash, but a safer six-house plan would leave $126.

Opponent p2 has $195 cash and two houses on each dark blue property. Their holdings include Park Place and Boardwalk, both at two houses. I am weighing this against the rent spike from adding a third house to Virginia Avenue.

p2 could mortgage a railroad for $100 and buy one more house on Boardwalk, raising its rent to $1400. That is dangerous.

p3 has only $53 and one house each on the red properties. He cannot build more houses easily.

p4 is rich with $1081 but in jail. He owns Mediterranean, New York Avenue, Ventnor, and North Carolina Avenue with no monopoly. He also holds a Get Out of Jail Free card.

I am not actually in jail. My position is simply the Jail square, and I can still take actions before ending my turn. The turn index shows 63, which means this is my new turn after the previous three turns were played by other players.

Mortgaging Connecticut Avenue would only yield $60, which is still too little to cover a $100 railroad rent. Selling houses later would be half price and must remain evenly balanced across the group.

I will build the seven houses now and mortgage Connecticut Avenue afterward for a cash buffer. Virginia Avenue should receive the third house because its rent spike is larger than the other two properties. Four houses on Virginia and three on the others would cost $1000, which exceeds my available cash.

I am now calculating the landing spaces from Jail. After rolling, I would land on St. Charles Place, States Avenue, or Virginia Avenue. I am also checking whether to build fewer houses to preserve cash.

Rolling from Jail lands on St. Charles, States, and Virginia. The next roll would hit Pennsylvania Railroad for $100, which is unaffordable with only $26 left after seven houses. Building six houses instead would leave $126 cash.

Building five houses would leave $226 cash but drop Virginia rent from $500 to $180. The seventh house adds $320 in rent potential, so the risk is worth it.

Opponent p2 is currently at Free Parking and not immediately threatening the pink properties.

Opponent p3 is in jail. When released, he will land on St. Charles Place, States Avenue, or Virginia Avenue immediately. With only $53 cash and three houses on Virginia Avenue, he could declare bankruptcy to me unless he raises funds first.

p3 cannot raise enough cash to pay a $500 rent on Virginia Avenue. Selling three houses from his red properties would yield only $225, and mortgaging the remaining reds plus Baltic, Oriental, and Vermont adds another $340. That brings his total to roughly $618, which is still below the $700 needed for seven houses on the pink set.

P3 can mortgage his light blue properties to survive a two-house pink rent of $150. He cannot afford a three-house Virginia rent of $500 without selling red houses.

P4 can pay a $500 Virginia rent, but that would still drain my cash. P2 is at Free Parking and poses no immediate threat. I will roll into the early side of the board and avoid the dark blue properties for now.

Building six houses would leave $126 cash, enough to cover the $100 Pennsylvania Railroad rent and the $90 Kentucky rent. The $26 balance from seven houses is too small for either. I will build six houses instead.

I am reconsidering the six-house plan. If I build seven houses and later hit a $100 rent, I can sell one house from Virginia Avenue to pay it, evens the set back to 2-2-2, and still keep a cash buffer. The extra rent potential from three houses on Virginia is worth that risk, especially since p3 and p4 are about to walk the pink properties before my next roll.

P3 likely cannot afford to pay $50 to get out of jail. He will probably try to roll doubles instead. A roll of 1 lands on St. Charles Place. A roll of 2 lands on the mortgaged Electric Company. A roll of 3 lands on States Avenue.

A roll of doubles from Jail lands on three of my pink properties. Three doubles out of six outcomes hit St. Charles Place, States Avenue, or Virginia Avenue. P3 has only $53 cash and one house each on the reds. Selling those three houses yields $225, bringing his total to $278. Mortgaging his light blue properties adds another $190, giving him roughly $468. That is still below the $700 needed for seven houses on the pink set.

P3 can raise $748 by mortgaging his light blue properties, so a $500 Virginia rent is survivable but leaves him bankrupted. I will build seven houses interleaved across the pink set.

Unmortgaging St. James, B&O, or PA is not worthwhile because they lack monopolies and the cost exceeds the rent benefit. I will keep Connecticut Avenue to block p3 from completing a cheap light blue monopoly.

I will not trade with p2 because they could use cash to build Boardwalk to three houses. Building is the only urgent action this turn, so I am submitting an interleaved build plan to keep the house counts within one of each other.

The interleaved build plan is now concrete: St. Charles Place, States Avenue, Virginia Avenue, St. Charles Place, States Avenue, Virginia Avenue, Virginia Avenue. This yields a 2-2-2 spread after six houses and a 3-2-2 spread after seven. The engine checks intermediate states, so strict alternation is required. I am also concerned the backend might group by property and sum counts before applying the plan.

A safer approach is to build one house on each property in separate decision rounds. This guarantees an even intermediate state regardless of how the engine batches the plan. The error message explicitly requires interleaving purchases across the group.

I am now weighing a safer strategy: building one house on each pink property in this single action. This guarantees an even intermediate state regardless of how the engine processes the plan, and the instructions confirm that multi-step post-turn actions are allowed. The downside is three extra round trips, but it eliminates the risk of wasting a turn if a large interleaved call fails.

I will attempt the full seven-house interleaved build now. If the engine rejects it for batching, I can retry one house at a time. I confirmed that seven houses cost $700 and leave $26 cash. I am ready to submit the plan.
